ALB.story:
The record for Albania comes mainly from the US State Department's 2025 Trafficking in Persons report, the US government's yearly review of how each country deals with trafficking. It says traffickers exploit Albanian women and children for sex and forced labour inside the country, especially during the tourist season. It also says Roma and Balkan-Egyptian children, from two minority communities, are forced to beg. Families are listed alongside traffickers among those who exploit children.

Albania also sends people abroad who are then exploited. The report says Albanian migrants in Western Europe, particularly the United Kingdom, are vulnerable to being forced into crime. In 2024 Albanians were the second most common nationality referred to the UK's system for identifying possible victims of trafficking, with 2,492 referrals, but 95 per cent of them were referred as adults, so the British figures say little about Albanian children.

Prosecution inside Albania has been rare. In the year the report covers, courts convicted two sex traffickers and two labour traffickers, the first trafficking convictions since 2021. The map counts this record among cases in which officials took part or looked away, and the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC), a research network, scores the presence of criminals inside the state at 6.5 out of 10. The US places Albania on Tier 2, meaning the government does not fully meet the US minimum standards but is making efforts. Walk Free, an anti-slavery organisation, estimates 34,000 people in modern slavery in Albania, of all ages and in all forms. In 2024 the US National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) received 5,906 reports of suspected online child sexual abuse traced to Albania, or 248.5 per 100,000 people.

Exploitation during the tourist season and forced begging continue, and convictions have only just resumed. The number of Albanian children exploited abroad is not known from these figures.

BFA.story:
In Burkina Faso the documented abuse of children is tied to armed conflict. The UN verified the abduction of 309 children in 2024. The armed group JNIM carried out 157 of these abductions and the armed group ISGS 80; unidentified perpetrators carried out 47, and 25 were carried out by the state's Defence and Security Forces or the Volunteers for the Defence of the Homeland (VDP), civilians armed to fight alongside the army. The UN also verified the rape of four girls that year, two of them by the VDP, and in 2022 it verified the rape of 16 girls, two by the Defence and Security Forces.

Burkinabè children are also moved across borders. Nigerian police said that some of the more than 300 boys and men freed in a 2019 raid on a building in Kaduna, northern Nigeria, signed as an Islamic studies centre, had been brought from Burkina Faso, Mali and Ghana. Many were chained; local media reported that captives were tortured, starved and sexually abused, and seven people who claimed to be teachers were arrested. Burkina Faso is also a destination. The US State Department's 2025 trafficking report says Nigerian networks move women and girls to mining regions in Senegal, Mali, Burkina Faso and Côte d'Ivoire.

The state's capacity to respond is rated low. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC), a research network, scores the trafficking market at 7 out of 10, the presence of criminals inside the state at 7, and the country's resilience to organised crime at 2.88 out of 10. The US places Burkina Faso on its Tier 2 Watch List, one step above the lowest rating. Walk Free, an anti-slavery organisation, estimates 77,000 people in modern slavery. NCMEC, the US child-protection centre, received 7,829 reports of suspected online child abuse traced to the country in 2024, but Childlight, a research institute, found no representative survey data on online child sexual exploitation for West and Central Africa.

Abductions by armed groups and by state auxiliaries continued through 2024. The extent of online abuse and of trafficking to the mines is not measured.

BTN.story:
The map holds no case, flow or network for Bhutan, so what is known comes from ratings and counts made from outside. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC), a research network, scores the human trafficking market at 6 out of 10 and the presence of criminals inside the state at 3, with a resilience to organised crime of 4.67 out of 10. The US State Department places Bhutan on Tier 2, meaning the government does not fully meet US minimum standards but is making efforts.

In 2024 the US National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) received 2,140 reports of suspected online child sexual abuse traced to Bhutan, or 270.4 per 100,000 people. Childlight, a research institute, found no representative survey data on online child sexual exploitation anywhere in South Asia.

What happens to children in Bhutan is largely unrecorded in the sources this map uses.

COD.story:
Most of the record for DR Congo concerns armed conflict in the east, where armed groups and the national army have recruited, abducted and raped children. The UN human rights office's Mapping Report of 2010, covering 1993 to 2003, described the apparent systematic use of rape, allegedly by all combatant forces, against women and girls, and found that child soldiers were raped and tortured in military camps; among the 12 parties it listed for recruiting children was the national army. In 2024 the UN verified sexual violence against 358 girls, by the armed groups M23 (68) and CODECO (63), the national army (47) and others, and the abduction of 815 children, 265 of them by the armed group ADF.

Some commanders from Ituri province have been tried by the International Criminal Court (ICC), the permanent international war crimes court. It convicted Thomas Lubanga in 2012 of conscripting and using children under 15; sexual violence against girl soldiers was raised at his trial but not charged. In 2019 it convicted Bosco Ntaganda of 18 counts, including rape and sexual slavery of child soldiers.

UN peacekeepers and aid workers have also abused children. In 2004 UN investigators found that sex with peacekeepers in Bunia occurred "with regularity", usually for food or small sums, and often involved girls under 18, some as young as 13; six cases were fully substantiated. In 2024 the UN still recorded 44 allegations in DR Congo and nine child victims in its mission there. Only the soldiers' home countries can prosecute them; the UN can only send them home. A commission appointed by the World Health Organization found in 2021 that during the 2018–2020 Ebola response, mostly temporary Congolese staff used their authority to obtain sex, often in exchange for jobs, from people as young as 13.

The US State Department's 2025 report says mining bosses, miners, family members, government officials and armed groups force children to work in eastern artisanal mines, that most trafficking is internal, including forced marriage of girls, and that official complicity contributed to impunity. The research network GI-TOC scores the presence of criminals inside the state at 9 out of 10. In addition, 3,483 children were adopted abroad from 2003 to 2022; the government suspended exit permits for them in 2013.

Abductions and sexual violence by armed groups and the army continued in 2024. More than 500 paternity claims against peacekeepers since 2006 are still pending.

DNK.story:
Three forms of child abuse appear in the Danish record: abuse in state institutions in the twentieth century, the adoption of foreign children whose papers had been falsified, and online abuse networks run from or traced to Denmark.

The state homes are documented by inquiries the government commissioned itself. The Godhavn Report of 2011 examined the Godhavn boys' home and 18 other state homes from 1945 to 1976 and found neglect and physical and sexual abuse. No prosecutions followed, and Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen apologised in 2019. A second investigation, published in 2022, covered særforsorgen, the state's special-care institutions for people with disabilities. It found widespread abuse, including sexual assault of children, from 1933 to 1980, and found that the state had not carried out systematic oversight. A minister apologised on the state's behalf in 2023.

Denmark was a receiving country for intercountry adoption. In all, 9,297 South Korean children were sent to Denmark from 1965 to 2008, and children also came from Sri Lanka in the 1980s. In 2024 the Appeals Board (Ankestyrelsen), the authority that supervises intercountry adoption, found "systematic illegal behaviour" on the Korean side in adoptions from 1970 to 1989. Children's identities and backgrounds were altered in official papers and large sums passed between agencies in the two countries. It found that the Danish agencies DanAdopt and AC Børnehjælp knew that children's information was being changed. In 2024 Denmark's only intercountry adoption agency said it was shutting down.

Danish police have been at the start of several international online cases. In the early 1990s US Customs traced abuse images to Bamse, a Danish bulletin board with about 900 users, which led to about 35 arrests and convictions in the US. In Operation Hamlet, announced in 2002, Danish police acting on information from Save the Children arrested a couple who had posted images of the abuse of their own daughter, and the inquiry led to a network in which many parents abused their own children; 45 children were rescued, 37 in the US. In 2025 Danish police led an operation in 19 countries against a paid platform on which a Danish man distributed AI-generated abuse material he had made; 273 suspects were identified and 25 arrested.

The institutional abuse ended decades ago; the state has apologised, and no prosecutions followed the Godhavn report. Adoptee groups say the 2024 adoption report left the Danish state's own role unexamined.

FIN.story:
The Finnish record concerns two settings in which adults with authority over children failed them: the state's child welfare care in the twentieth century, and a large religious movement that handled abuse inside its own community.

A study for the Ministry of Social Affairs and Health interviewed about 300 people who had been placed in child welfare substitute care, meaning children's homes and foster families, between 1937 and 1983. It found maltreatment and violence in all forms of care. The Finnish government apologised officially on 20 November 2016.

The second setting is the Conservative Laestadian movement, Finland's largest revivalist movement within the Lutheran church, with about 35,000 members. In 2011 its central body, the SRK, announced that an internal report had found 70 to 100 cases of child sexual abuse within the movement since the 1980s. Most involved abuse within member families rather than by church officials. The SRK admitted that its officials had mishandled the cases, had not used expert help and lacked the knowledge to respond. A study of abuse in the movement by Johanna Hurtig of the University of Tampere was published the same year.

Finland is also linked to international online abuse networks on this map, including the Wonderland Club, broken up in 1998, the paid streaming site Kidflix, closed in 2025, and a Danish-run platform for AI-generated abuse material, closed the same year; the sources do not describe Finland's part in them. In 2024 the US National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) received 15,726 reports of suspected online child sexual abuse traced to Finland, or 279.8 per 100,000 people. The US State Department rates Finland Tier 1, and the research network GI-TOC scores its resilience to organised crime at 8.42 out of 10.

The state has apologised for abuse in care, and the SRK has admitted mishandling cases. The map holds no record of prosecutions arising from either.

GMB.story:
The main form of child sexual exploitation on record in The Gambia is the sale of children to foreign tourists. The US State Department's 2025 trafficking report says European tourists, primarily from the United Kingdom, reportedly travel to The Gambia to exploit children, and that organised networks use European and Gambian travel agencies to promote the country as a destination, especially the Senegambia Strip. Women and girls from other West African countries, especially Nigeria, are recruited for jobs in tourism and then sexually exploited.

The law was changed to reach the hotels. The Tourism Offences Act of 2003 defines a child as anyone under 18, makes hotel operators liable if they knowingly allow child prostitution, and provides life imprisonment for child trafficking by tourists. By 2017 the US report said traffickers increasingly hosted child sex tourists in private homes outside the commercial tourist areas, where detection is harder.

The Gambia also appears in the record as a country children were adopted from. After reports of malpractice in adoptions from Ethiopia, the Flemish government in Belgium had an expert panel review intercountry adoption, and the screening of every country of origin that followed led Flanders to stop adoptions from Gambia, among others. The sources on the map do not say what was found about Gambian adoptions.

The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC), a research network, scores the trafficking market at 6 out of 10 and the presence of criminals inside the state at 7. The US places The Gambia on Tier 2. Walk Free, an anti-slavery organisation, estimates 16,000 people in modern slavery. The US child-protection centre NCMEC received 1,188 reports of suspected online child abuse traced to the country in 2024, and Childlight, a research institute, found no representative survey data on online exploitation for West and Central Africa.

Exploitation by tourists continues, now more often in private homes. How many children are involved is not known.

HND.story:
Two groups exploit children in Honduras in the record on this map: gangs at home and men who come from North America. The US State Department's 2025 trafficking report says criminal organisations, including gangs, exploit girls in sex trafficking in Honduran cities, and that men from Canada and the United States exploit Honduran children.

Charity work has given foreign offenders access to children. A Pennsylvania priest, Fr Joseph Maurizio, abused minors on charity trips to an orphanage in El Progreso between 2004 and 2009, paid for partly through illegal money transfers; a US court convicted him in 2015.

A US prosecution shows how women and girls from the region have been taken north. The Rendon-Reyes organisation, a family network based in Tenancingo, Mexico, smuggled women and girls from Mexico and Central America into the United States from 2004 to 2015 and forced them into prostitution; five members were sentenced in New York in 2019. The US prosecutors' statement says "Central America" without naming countries, so it does not establish that Honduran girls were among the victims.

The state is rated as weak against organised crime. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC), a research network, scores the presence of criminals inside the state at 8.5 out of 10, the trafficking market at 7.5, and the country's resilience to organised crime at 3.92. The US places Honduras on Tier 2. Walk Free, an anti-slavery organisation, estimates 69,000 people in modern slavery. In 2024 the US National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) received 34,007 reports of suspected online child sexual abuse traced to Honduras, or 314.1 per 100,000 people.

Gang exploitation of girls and abuse by visiting North Americans are both described as current. The map holds few Honduran prosecutions, and the scale is not known.

IRQ.story:
The largest part of the Iraqi record is the capture and sale of Yazidi women and children by the Islamic State group (ISIS) from 2014. ISIS attacked the Sinjar area on 3 August 2014 and moved captives in an organised way, by bus and truck, to holding sites in Tal Afar, Mosul and Baaj. Women and girls were then taken to Raqqa in Syria. The UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria found in June 2016 that ISIS had committed genocide against the Yazidis. Women and girls, some as young as nine, were sold at market and held as sexual slaves, and boys were forced into ISIS training camps. At that date more than 3,200 Yazidi women and children were still held, mostly in Syria, and thousands remain missing.

Armed groups still take children, on a smaller scale. The UN verified the abduction of 18 children in Iraq in 2022, 10 of them by ISIS and four by the armed group HPG/PKK, and of eight in 2024, two boys by ISIS and six girls by HPG/PKK, mostly to recruit and use them.

Since the war, officials are alleged to exploit displaced families. The US State Department's 2025 trafficking report says women and girls in camps for displaced people whose relatives have alleged ISIS ties may face sexual exploitation by security and military officials. An international organisation reported in 2024 that officials coerce relatives of detained children into sex in exchange for security clearances or civil documents; the government reported no action against officials. The report adds that Yazidi survivors remain at risk of being trafficked again. The UN also recorded one child victim of sexual exploitation in 2024 in UNITAD, its own mission in Iraq.

The research network GI-TOC scores the presence of criminals inside the Iraqi state at 8.5 out of 10 and the country's resilience to organised crime at 3.33. Walk Free, an anti-slavery organisation, estimates 221,000 people in modern slavery. In 2024 the US National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) received 407,432 reports of suspected online child sexual abuse traced to Iraq, or 884.9 per 100,000 people, while Childlight, a research institute, found no representative survey data on online exploitation for the Middle East and North Africa.

Thousands of Yazidis taken in 2014 are still missing. Abuse of displaced families by officials is alleged and has not been acted on, and no survey explains the high number of online reports.

KAZ.story:
Two forms appear in the record for Kazakhstan: the recruitment of rural girls for sexual exploitation in cities and abroad, and the adoption of children by foreign families.

The US State Department's 2025 trafficking report says traffickers lure girls and women from rural Kazakhstan, and from neighbouring Central Asian, East Asian and Eastern European countries, with offers of work as waitresses, models or nannies in large cities, including through social media. Kazakh women and girls are also exploited in Russia, Uzbekistan, the Middle East, Europe, East Asia and the United States.

Kazakhstan has sent large numbers of children abroad for adoption, and the route remains open. The US issued 6,612 immigrant visas to children adopted from Kazakhstan between 1994 and 2014, with a peak of 826 in 2004, and an adoption researcher, Selman, counts 6,541 children sent abroad from 2003 to 2022. The map holds no finding of fraud in these adoptions.

The research network GI-TOC scores the trafficking market at 6 out of 10 and the presence of criminals inside the state at 6. The US places Kazakhstan on Tier 2. Walk Free, an anti-slavery organisation, estimates 208,000 people in modern slavery, or 11.1 per 1,000 people. In 2024 the US National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) received 119,176 reports of suspected online child sexual abuse traced to Kazakhstan, or 578.7 per 100,000 people.

Recruitment of girls to cities and abroad is described as current. How many children are affected, and what lies behind the high number of online reports, is not recorded.

LBY.story:
Libya's place in the record is as a transit country on the route from sub-Saharan Africa to Europe, where migrant girls and young women are sexually exploited on the way.

Inside Libya, the US State Department's 2025 trafficking report says commercial sex rings hold sub-Saharan women and girls in brothels, particularly in the southern towns of Ubari, Sabha and Murzuq, and that Nigerian women and girls are at increased risk. It cites an international organisation's finding that 77 per cent of children and young people crossing Libya showed signs of exploitation that amount to trafficking.

The route leads to Italy. In 2017 the International Organization for Migration (IOM), the UN migration agency, said that perhaps 80 per cent of Nigerian women and girls arriving in Italy by sea could be sex-trafficking victims; by its indicators most victims were aged 13 to 24. Nigerian female arrivals rose from 1,500 in 2014 to more than 11,000 in 2016, according to IOM data.

Officials are reported to take part. Observers cited by the US report describe systemic complicity by the Libyan Coast Guard and by immigration and security officials, and the government has never reported prosecuting or convicting anyone for sex or labour trafficking. The US lists Libya as a "special case" rather than giving it a tier. The research network GI-TOC scores the presence of criminals inside the state at 9.5 out of 10, the trafficking market at 8.5, and the country's resilience to organised crime at 1.88. In 2024 the US National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) received 50,742 reports of suspected online child abuse traced to Libya, and Childlight, a research institute, found no representative survey data on online exploitation for the region.

The brothels in the south and the route north are described as active, and no trafficker is known to have been convicted in Libya.

MEX.story:
The Mexican record has three main parts: abuse by Catholic clergy that church authorities handled internally, private shelters where children placed by the state were abused or disappeared, and family networks that trafficked girls and women to brothels in the United States.

The Legion of Christ, a religious order founded in Mexico in 1941 by Marcial Maciel, is the clearest case of protection. Letters to the Vatican in 1976, 1978 and 1989 and formal charges in 1998 produced no action; in 2010 the Vatican said the Legion had shielded him. The order's own 2019 report found that 33 of its priests had abused 175 minors since 1941, at least 60 of them abused by Maciel. Prosecutors opened 156 investigations into sexual offences by religious figures from 2009 to 2019, and four prosecutors' offices recorded only six sentences. The Mexican Episcopal Conference, the national bishops' body, said in 2019 there was no national count of victims because each bishop handles cases himself.

Private shelters held children with little check by the authorities, even after complaints. In 2014 federal prosecutors raided La Gran Familia, a shelter in Zamora, and freed 432 children and 138 adults; residents reported rape, confinement, hunger and forced begging, and more than 40 complaints from parents had been filed with the authorities before the raid. In 2009 children placed by Mexico City prosecutors in the Casitas del Sur shelter went missing; a city legislator accused prosecutors' staff of warning the shelter before searches.

Officials are also accused of protecting an exploitation ring. The Cancún hotelier Jean Succar Kuri was convicted in 2011 after complaints by several girls. The journalist Lydia Cacho, whose 2005 book linked him to the businessman Kamel Nacif and the Puebla governor Mario Marín, was then arrested by Puebla police; leaked calls recorded the two men discussing jailing her as a favour. Marín was arrested in 2021 and is on trial for her alleged torture; neither man has been convicted, and both are accused of torture, not of the abuse itself.

From 1991 to 2004 the Carreto family of Tenancingo, Tlaxcala, recruited poor women and girls by deception and forced them into prostitution in New York; two brothers received 50-year sentences in the US.

In the figures on record few clergy cases ended in a conviction, and no national count of church victims exists. In 2010 the 14 children missing from Casitas del Sur were still being sought.

MWI.story:
The main form of child exploitation on record in Malawi is the recruitment of girls for sex in and around Dzaleka refugee camp. The US State Department's 2025 trafficking report says the camp holds about 53,000 refugees in a space built for 10,000, and that organised transnational syndicates working from informal bars and housing inside it recruit girls for sex trafficking in the camp and in roadside bars along the highway to Lilongwe. Girls are also exploited in bars and illegal brothels in Lilongwe and Blantyre.

The camp is also a stopping point on what the report calls the Southern Route. Criminal networks move migrants through Dzaleka towards South Africa, where some end up in sex trafficking or forced labour. The report says official complicity continued to hold back enforcement.

Malawi has also served as a refuge for a foreign abuser. The Slovenian priest Franc Frantar, detained in 2006 for abusing up to 16 minors, first avoided prosecution by going to Malawi as a missionary and returned to Slovenia only after Interpol, the international police organisation, issued a notice; he was later sentenced, with sources giving terms of three and a half and five years.

The research network GI-TOC scores the trafficking market at 5 out of 10 and the presence of criminals inside the state at 4. The US places Malawi on Tier 2. Walk Free, an anti-slavery organisation, estimates 93,000 people in modern slavery. The US National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) received 2,774 reports of suspected online child abuse traced to Malawi in 2024, or 12.8 per 100,000 people.

Recruitment of girls around Dzaleka is described as current, and the number of girls affected is not known.

NZL.story:
Most of the New Zealand record concerns children abused while in the care of the state or of churches. The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care reported in 2024 that an estimated 200,000 of about 655,000 people in state and faith-based care between 1950 and 2019 were abused, that sexual abuse was commonplace and that Māori were more likely to be abused. It found that the state failed to respond to signs of systemic abuse.

In one state hospital, the commission found, children were tortured. Of the 362 children who went through the child and adolescent unit at Lake Alice, a state psychiatric hospital, between 1972 and 1978, about half were Māori boys; survivors described electric shocks without anaesthetic as punishment, and evidence was given of rape by staff and adult patients. The psychiatrist Selwyn Leeks denied abuse and was never charged in New Zealand. Only after the UN Committee Against Torture found in 2019 that New Zealand had failed to investigate did police open a new investigation, in 2020, and in 2024 the government offered NZ$150,000 to each survivor.

Church bodies moved accused abusers to new posts. The St John of God Brothers, a Catholic order, ran Marylands, a Christchurch school for boys with learning disabilities, where more than one in five of 537 boys reported abuse between 1955 and 1984. The order moved Brother Bernard McGrath to Australia after allegations in 1977; he has been convicted of more than 100 offences in the two countries. The commission found the Catholic Church transferred abusers to other ministries, where they offended again, and recommended investigating priests sent to Papua New Guinea. In 2022 the church admitted that 14 per cent of its diocesan clergy had been accused since 1950. At Dilworth, an Anglican-linked Auckland boarding school for boys from poor families, an inquiry found sexual abuse from the mid-1950s to 2005; police estimated 233 victims.

New Zealand also acts against offenders abroad and online. A 2005 law made sexual conduct with children abroad by citizens and residents a crime. The Department of Internal Affairs led an investigation from 2019 into people exchanging images of the abuse of infants, which by 2022 had led to 46 arrests in New Zealand and 146 children safeguarded worldwide.

Lake Alice survivors have been offered redress. For others in care, the commissioners found in 2024 very little progress on the redress system they had recommended in 2021.

PRI.story:
The record for Puerto Rico, a US territory in the Caribbean, concerns sexual abuse by Catholic priests and how the church dealt with the state's investigators. In early 2014, after reports in the newspaper El Nuevo Día, Bishop Daniel Fernández of the Arecibo diocese disclosed that since 2011 he had expelled six priests accused of sexual abuse.

The disclosure led to a wider criminal inquiry. Local prosecutors said at least 11 other priests on the island were under investigation, the Justice Secretary said at least four dioceses were being investigated, and US Homeland Security Investigations, a federal agency, requested information. Prosecutor Yolanda Pitino said the diocese's information was insufficient and that it had not answered requests for more, and Justice Secretary César Miranda warned that he might charge church officials suspected of withholding information.

The map holds no later outcome of the inquiry and no other form of child exploitation for the island. The research network GI-TOC scores the trafficking market at 6.5 out of 10 and resilience to organised crime at 6.96. In 2024 the US National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) received 5,960 reports of suspected online child abuse traced to Puerto Rico, or 186.1 per 100,000 people.

What the 2014 investigation of the dioceses produced is not recorded here.

RWA.story:
The map holds no case or flow for Rwanda. Its one entry concerns intercountry adoption: on 10 October 2007 Ireland's Adoption Board, the authority then responsible for foreign adoptions, suspended adoptions from Ethiopia and Rwanda. The record here does not give the reason.

The other information is ratings and counts. The research network GI-TOC scores the human trafficking market at 5.5 out of 10 and the presence of criminals inside the state at 6. The US State Department places Rwanda on its Tier 2 Watch List, one step above the lowest rating. Walk Free, an anti-slavery organisation, estimates 55,000 people in modern slavery. The US National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) received 2,020 reports of suspected online child abuse traced to Rwanda in 2024, or 14.2 per 100,000 people.

How children are exploited in Rwanda is not described in the sources this map uses.

SSD.story:
In South Sudan the documented sexual abuse of girls is carried out mostly by armed forces during the country's conflict, and the national army is the largest single perpetrator in the UN's counts. The UN verified sexual violence against 94 girls, some as young as seven, in 2022; 74 of these cases were by the South Sudan People's Defence Forces (SSPDF), the state's army, and others by factions of the opposition SPLM/A-IO and by the national police. In 2024 it verified sexual violence against seven girls, five by the SSPDF.

The UN Commission on Human Rights in South Sudan reported in 2022 that parties to the conflict used the rape of women and girls as a means of terror and political repression. It found that abductions of women and girls for forced marriage and sexual slavery had increased in Jonglei, the Greater Pibor Administrative Area, Warrap and Lakes. The commission described impunity for armed forces in Western Equatoria, and noted that although a military court in Yei convicted SSPDF soldiers of rape in late 2020, the victims had not received the compensation the court ordered.

Some of those sent to help displaced people are accused of exploiting them. A 2022 investigation by The New Humanitarian and Al Jazeera reported that from 2015 to 2022 aid workers in the UN-run camp for displaced people at Malakal exploited women and girls, including by demanding sex in exchange for aid; staff of IOM, MSF, WFP and World Vision were among those named. The UN recorded two child victims of its own peacekeeping mission in South Sudan in 2024.

The Lord's Resistance Army (LRA), a Ugandan armed group, held abducted Ugandan children at bases in southern Sudan from 1994 to 2006, and from 2008 abducted thousands more in South Sudan and neighbouring countries.

The US State Department ranks South Sudan on Tier 3, its lowest rating, and the research network GI-TOC scores the presence of criminals inside the state at 9 out of 10. Only 863 reports of suspected online child abuse traced to South Sudan reached the US National Center for Missing & Exploited Children in 2024; the map counts South Sudan among the places from which almost no reports reach the international systems.

Abductions and sexual violence by armed forces and groups were still being verified in 2024, and the compensation ordered in Yei had not been paid when the commission reported.

THA.story:
The largest part of the Thai record is the sexual exploitation of children by foreign men who travel to the country, often in bars and tourist districts. A Swiss man already convicted of abusing children at home in 1980 and 1991 returned to Thailand in 1996 and, mainly from 2002 to 2013, abused more than 80 boys in Pattaya, where he ran a bar with a hotel room used by Europeans, and in the north; he also forced boys to perform sexual acts with European clients. Mark Frost, a former British teacher and scout leader, abused boys from poor families in Thailand from 2011 to 2013 and streamed abuse by webcam to another European man. Both were tried in their home countries; Frost received 13 life terms in 2017, and Britain's Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse counted his among only about eight successful UK prosecutions since 1997 for offences committed abroad.

Thailand has tightened its laws and enforcement. A 1996 law made sex with anyone under 18 in a prostitution establishment a crime regardless of consent, and in 2017 Thailand refused entry to 74 known foreign sex offenders. A 2023 raid on an illegal bar on Bangla Road in Patong, Phuket, freed six children under 18; in 2024 a Phuket court sentenced seven defendants, the foreign owner to a total of 1,073 years. Five senior Patong police officers were transferred after the raid.

Children are also brought into the trade from neighbouring countries. The US State Department's 2025 trafficking report says children from Thailand, Burma, Cambodia and Laos are increasingly sex-trafficked in brothels, massage parlours, bars, karaoke lounges and hotels, and that many Lao women and girls are exploited in Thailand.

Abuse is also produced in Thailand for viewers online. In Operation Blackwrist, run by INTERPOL, the international police organisation, the abuse of 11 boys under 13 was found published weekly on a subscription website with nearly 63,000 users; a Thai court sentenced its main administrator to 146 years in 2018. In 2024 the US National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) received 276,031 reports of suspected online child abuse traced to Thailand. Separately, an adoption researcher, Selman, counts 6,478 Thai children adopted abroad from 2003 to 2022.

The US report describes the sex trafficking of children in bars and brothels as rising in 2025. How many children are involved is not recorded.

UGA.story:
From 1987 the main form of child abuse on record in Uganda was abduction by the Lord's Resistance Army (LRA), an armed group. It took tens of thousands of children from northern Uganda to serve as fighters, porters and "wives"; UNICEF estimated at least 25,000 by 2006, and abducted children were held at LRA bases in southern Sudan. The International Criminal Court (ICC) convicted the commander Dominic Ongwen, himself abducted as a child, in 2021 of 61 crimes including rape, sexual slavery, forced marriage and the use of children under 15, and sentenced him to 25 years.

Today the record points to the Karamoja region in the north-east. The US State Department's 2025 trafficking report says non-governmental organisations estimate that most child sex-trafficking victims in Uganda are Karamojong, especially from Napak district. Traffickers, sometimes community elders, make children meet them at international borders, where markets are organised to sell them into domestic servitude or sex trafficking. Cross-border rings take women and underage girls from Karamoja to Nairobi in Kenya, and women, girls and boys are exploited in brothels, bars and homes in Kampala.

Many children in Uganda's children's homes have living families, and such homes have been used to supply foreign adoptions. The Ministry of Gender, Labour and Social Development says only 185 children's homes are fully licensed and more than 500 operate without oversight; its principal probation officer said many children in homes are not orphans. Between 2013 and 2016 an Ohio agency, European Adoption Consultants, arranged the adoption of more than 30 Ugandan children by US families after their own families had been promised the children would go to school in Kampala. One employee pleaded guilty in 2019 to bribing Ugandan officials, others were charged in 2020, and the US government sanctioned two Ugandan judges and two lawyers.

Ugandan soldiers abroad have also been accused. Human Rights Watch documented in 2014 that African Union soldiers in Somalia, mainly Ugandans at the mission's headquarters, sexually abused and exploited women and girls who came to the bases for medicine or aid; four rapes and one sexual assault involved girls under 18.

The research network GI-TOC scores the presence of criminals inside the Ugandan state at 8 out of 10. The sale of Karamojong children is described as current. The government has closed some unregistered homes; more than 500 were operating without oversight when the ministry reported.

WSM.story:
The main case on record for Samoa is the removal of children through intercountry adoption under false pretences. From 2002 to 2005 Focus on Children, an adoption agency in Utah in the United States run by Scott and Karen Banks, arranged about 80 adoptions of Samoan children. The parents were told their children would go to the US for a time to attend school; the children were in fact adopted permanently.

The US federal courts dealt with the case as an immigration matter. A 2007 indictment charged the Banks couple and three others with alien smuggling, visa fraud and money laundering. In 2009 all of them pleaded guilty to misdemeanour counts of aiding the improper entry of an alien, and the agency to a felony conspiracy; the judge sentenced them to five years' probation and banned them from adoption work.

Samoa also appears as a place where an abuser was sent from abroad. A Salesian priest, a member of a Catholic religious order, who had been convicted of abuse in Melbourne, Australia, was allegedly moved to Samoa to avoid further police investigation.

The research network GI-TOC scores the human trafficking market at 3 out of 10 and the presence of criminals inside the state at 2.5. The map has no US State Department trafficking rating for Samoa. The US National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) received 260 reports of suspected online child abuse traced to Samoa in 2024, or 119.3 per 100,000 people.

The Banks couple are barred from adoption work. The record does not say whether the Samoan children were reunited with their families.
